topic.title: Translation
topic.shortdesc: How translates DITA content with a steerable AI agent, reusing previous translations so each job only handles what changed.

body.p: translates your DITA content into other languages with an AI translation agent. Two things make it distinctive:

ul.li: It is incremental. records what it has already translated, so re-running translation only reprocesses the files whose source changed. You do not pay to retranslate content that has not changed.

It is steerable. Rather than a fixed machine-translation pipeline, the agent follows guidance you provide, such as approved terminology, house style, and rules for your own DITA specializations, so output stays consistent across every language and every job.

body.p: To try it end to end, follow the Getting Started with Translation walkthrough, which uses a ready-made sample project.

section.title: The Translation Workflow
section.p: At a high level, translating content in works like this:

ol.li: In your workspace, you choose what to translate (one or more publications) and the target languages.
This starts one or more translation jobs, processed by the AI translation agent in the background.
Once the jobs finish, you bring the translated files into your workspace.
Review them and make any manual corrections you need.
Commit the result to your project's repository.

section.p: Because keeps a translation index in your repository, translation state travels with the content and later jobs only retranslate what changed. See Running an Incremental Translation.
Translation draws on your organization's AI Credits, and its incremental design keeps costs down by reprocessing only what changed.

section.title: A Steerable Translation Agent
section.p: You can steer how the agent translates content for your project, for example by supplying approved terminology, a style guide, or a list of strings that should never be translated. You can put the guidance in a file inside your project, and it applies to every job and every user until you change it. Because the agent reads whatever files you point it to, it can work with the formats your localization team already uses, whether that is a terminology file in a format like TBX (TermBase eXchange) or the custom strings files behind an application's UI. See Customizing the Translation Behavior.

section.title: You Stay in Control of Your Content
section.p: Translation is a reviewed, revertible workflow. To translate content, sends source content to an AI provider engaged under zero-data-retention terms, and the translated files it produces are proposed in your workspace for you to review before anything is committed. See Data Handling and Your Responsibilities for where your content goes and what to check before you commit.

Your translated files and translation state live in your own Git repository as plain, human-readable files, versioned under the same access control as the rest of your content. Nothing is locked inside a separate proprietary system.

section.title: Supported Languages
section.p: You can translate into any language identified by a BCP 47 language tag (for example fr, fr-FR, or de-DE); there is no fixed list of supported languages.

section.title: Current Limitations
section.p: The following are not supported today:

ul.li: Markdown files. They are neither translated nor copied into the target language folders; only DITA content is processed.
Translating text embedded in raster images or other binary assets. Text inside SVG graphics is copied unchanged by default, but you can opt in to translating it.
Exchanging translations with external translation management systems or translation agencies through XLIFF. Translations are produced and reviewed inside rather than exported to an outside tool.
Translation memories are not used during the translation process, nor generated afterwards.
